chief_complaint: sharp right upper quadrant abdominal pain after eating dinner
hpi_details: 6-hour history of steady, severe RUQ pain that began 1 hour after eating a fried chicken dinner. Pain radiates to the right shoulder blade. Associated with nausea and two episodes of bilious vomiting. Subjective fever at home. No jaundice or dark urine.
ideas: thinks she might have severe food poisoning from the dinner
concerns: worried because the pain is getting sharper when she takes a deep breath
expectations: wants strong pain relief and an ultrasound to see what is happening
pmh: obesity (BMI 32), hypercholesterolaemia, type 2 diabetes controlled with diet
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks wine socially on weekends, works as an accountant

investigation_events.title: STAT acute cholecystitis workup
investigation_events.availability_message: The STAT laboratory and right-upper-quadrant ultrasound results are now available; analgesia, fluids, and surgical consultation should not be delayed.

results.value: Multiple gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening to 5 mm, trace pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign; common bile duct 5 mm

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Cholecystitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes keeping the patient NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, IV analgesia and antiemetics, and empiric IV antibiotics (e.g., co-amoxiclav), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sharp right upper quadrant abdominal pain after eating dinner

Key HPI features: 6-hour history of steady, severe RUQ pain that began 1 hour after eating a fried chicken dinner. Pain radiates to the right shoulder blade. Associated with nausea and two episodes of bilious vomiting. Subjective fever at home. No jaundice or dark urine.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals needed (check for pyrexia/tachycardia). Abdominal exam for RUQ tenderness and Murphy's sign. Bloods: FBC (WBC), CRP, LFTs (lipase/amylase to exclude pancreatitis), abdominal ultrasound.
Relevant background/PMH: obesity (BMI 32), hypercholesterolaemia, type 2 diabetes controlled with diet
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Cholecystitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Biliary colic without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with right-upper-quadrant pain — suggests progression beyond simple biliary colic.
management_principles: Keep NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, IV analgesia and antiemetics, empiric IV antibiotics (e.g., co-amoxiclav), urgent RUQ ultrasound, surgical consultation for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 52F presenting with 6-hr severe RUQ pain radiating to right scapula postprandial (fatty meal). Nausea and vomiting x2. Positive inspiratory arrest (Murphy's sign history). No jaundice.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals needed (check for pyrexia/tachycardia). Abdominal exam for RUQ tenderness and Murphy's sign. Bloods: FBC (WBC), CRP, LFTs (lipase/amylase to exclude pancreatitis), abdominal ultrasound.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute cholecystitis secondary to cholelithiasis. DDx: biliary colic, acute pancreatitis, peptic ulcer perforation, right lower lobe pneumonia.
reference_soap.plan: Keep NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, IV analgesia and antiemetics, empiric IV antibiotics (e.g., co-amoxiclav), urgent RUQ ultrasound, surgical consultation for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

learning_objectives: Elicit classical biliary pain characteristics including radiation to scapula and postprandial onset
Identify risk factors for gallstone disease (female, fertile/fifties, fat)
Differentiate acute cholecystitis from uncomplicated biliary colic by duration and systemic signs
Explain NPO status and need for surgical evaluation clearly

teaching.one_liner: Gallstones block the cystic duct and the gallbladder becomes inflamed, causing steady right-upper-quadrant pain after fatty meals, often with fever.
red_flags: Fever with right-upper-quadrant pain — suggests progression beyond simple biliary colic

must_ask.say: Did the pain start after eating a fatty or fried meal?
Has this pain lasted for hours, rather than easing off after a few minutes?

must_ask.objective: Radiation to the shoulder or back
must_ask.say: Does the pain spread to your shoulder blade or your back?
Have you had a fever or chills with this?
Have you felt sick or vomited?
Have you noticed your skin or eyes turning yellow, or your urine going dark?
Does it hurt more when you take a deep breath in?

history.answer: I have this severe, sharp pain in the upper right side of my stomach that started a few hours after dinner.
It started about six hours ago, roughly an hour after I finished dinner, and it came on pretty suddenly.
The pain is right under my ribs on the upper right side, and it has stayed in that exact spot without moving elsewhere.
Yes, it radiates straight through to my back and up to my right shoulder blade.
It is a sharp, constant, aching pain. It does not come and go in waves; it just stays severe.
It is an 8 out of 10 on the pain scale. It built up rapidly and has stayed intensely severe the whole time.
Moving around makes it hurt worse, and nothing I have tried has eased it. Lying very still helps a tiny bit, but it is still awful.
Yes, whenever I take a deep breath in, the pain catches sharply right under my right ribs.
I have had mild stomach tightness or indigestion after heavy meals before, but never anything nearly this severe or prolonged.
I felt very nauseous and vomited twice. It was bitter, greenish-yellow liquid with no blood.
My bowel movements have been normal with no diarrhea, black stools, or blood, and I am still able to pass gas.
I felt quite feverish and had chills while at home, though I did not check my temperature with a thermometer.
No, my skin and the whites of my eyes look normal, my urine is not dark, and my stools have not looked pale.
I have no pain or burning when I urinate, no need to go more frequently, and no blood in my urine.
No, I have not felt dizzy, lightheaded, or like I was about to faint.
No, I do not have any vaginal bleeding or abnormal discharge.
I do not have chest pressure or tightness, and I am not short of breath other than finding it hard to take a deep breath because of the belly pain.
I had fried chicken and fries about an hour before the pain began, and I have not had any alcohol tonight.
I took an antacid tablet at home, but it did not help at all. I have not taken aspirin or painkillers like ibuprofen.
No, I have never had an irregular heart rhythm, palpitations, or any blood vessel problems.
I was thinking maybe I got a bad case of food poisoning from the fried chicken dinner.
I am really worried because the pain catches and gets so sharp every time I take a breath.
I really need strong pain relief right away, and I was hoping to get an ultrasound to find out what is happening inside.
I have high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes, which I manage with diet alone.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been hospitalized.
I take atorvastatin 20 milligrams once every evening, and no other prescription medications or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco.
I drink wine socially on weekends, usually one or two glasses.
I work as an accountant and live with my husband.
My mother had her gallbladder removed due to gallstones when she was in her fifties, and my father had high blood pressure.
I went through menopause two years ago and have had no periods since, so there is no possibility of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Patient appears uncomfortable and in acute distress from pain, lying still on the examination bed.
Blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, pulse 102 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 38.1°C, SpO2 98% on room air.
Sclerae are anicteric without yellowing; conjunctivae are pink without pallor.
Tachycardic regular rhythm; normal heart sounds S1 and S2 with no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Clear breath sounds throughout both lung fields without wheezes or crackles.
Abdomen is mildly obese, symmetric, and flat, with no surgical scars, visible pulsations, or caput medusae.
Hypoactive bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants; no bruits heard over the aorta or renal arteries.
Severe tenderness and voluntary guarding localized to the right upper quadrant; remaining quadrants are soft and non-tender.
Sharp inspiratory arrest elicited during deep palpation of the right upper quadrant beneath the costal margin.
No rebound tenderness and no abdominal wall rigidity.
No tenderness at McBurney's point; psoas, obturator, and Rovsing signs are negative.
No tenderness to gentle percussion at the bilateral costovertebral angles.
Normal anal sphincter tone, no rectal masses or tenderness, and stool is brown with no blood.
